responses.strategic_rationale: This 3-year residential parasomnia research unit navigates a core tension between naturalistic data capture and operational burden. Traditional polysomnography misses infrequent events; residential monitoring with continuous low-burden sensors and strategic enhanced nights captures behavior in a domestic-like environment, but staffing, participant retention, and false-alarm annotation create cascading costs. The chosen levers address critical trade-offs: balancing safety infrastructure against behavioral suppression, right-sizing the sensory montage for each night type, managing staff workload through semi-automation, controlling participant flow given limited event yield, and securing sustainable funding without losing academic independence. These five levers determine whether the facility validates a methodologically sound approach or becomes operationally unscalable.

levers.name: Safety-to-Naturalism Balance in Environmental Design
levers.consequences: Padded corridors and restricted windows prevent injuries but risk signaling 'clinical' context that suppresses spontaneous parasomnia expression. Conversely, minimizing visible safety cues may increase injury risk and liability exposure, forcing trade-offs between ecological validity and duty of care during unpredictable nocturnal events.
options: Maintain unobtrusive safety (soft-edge furniture, concealed door sensors, ambient lighting) and accept elevated insurance and incident-response protocols to preserve naturalistic sleep behavior.
Deploy visible safety features (padded walls, prominent signage, locked windows) and accept potential suppression of parasomnia frequency, requiring longer stays to capture equivalent event counts.
Implement a hybrid two-tier model: visible safety only in sleeping quarters, naturalistic domestic décor in common areas, with restricted participant movement between zones to segment risk exposure.
levers.review_lever: Visible safety measures deter parasomnia expression, prolonging stays and increasing cost-per-event; invisible safety reduces suppression but raises incident liability. The two-tier model adds complexity and staff enforcement overhead, limiting its scalability across 8+ suites without strict zoning protocols.

levers.name: Sensor Montage Stratification Across Stay Phases
levers.consequences: Dry-electrode EEG headbands and contactless sensors reduce setup burden and may improve compliance on routine nights, but lack the physiological sensitivity of standard PSG scalp electrodes for detecting subtle EEG signatures. Full montage every night is exhausting for participants and unsustainable for technician annotation; selective enhanced nights risk missing rare, unpredictable events.
options: Deploy full PSG montage every night for all participants, accepting higher technician workload, participant discomfort, and operational bottleneck in electrode fitting and removal, but ensuring no event is under-instrumented.

Restrict full PSG to the first, mid-stay, and final nights per protocol, accepting risk that spontaneous events on routine low-burden nights are captured at reduced fidelity and may be scored with lower confidence by independent raters.

Use real-time technician judgment to escalate montage based on observed movement clusters or environmental triggers, introducing subjective decision-making variability but allowing adaptive resource allocation.
levers.review_lever: Full nightly PSG guarantees fidelity but creates participant burden that may shorten stays and raise dropout rates. Protocol-scheduled enhanced nights offer efficiency but miss spontaneous events; escalation-triggered montage introduces rater bias and requires reliable technician pattern recognition under fatigue.

levers.name: Manual Annotation Bottleneck and Semi-Automated Triage Adoption
levers.consequences: Dual-rater AASM-criteria scoring ensures methodological rigor but requires hundreds of hours of expert time; with estimated 70–80% of participants producing at least one event per 2–8 week stay across 50–70 admitted participants, the annotation burden compounds rapidly. Semi-automated triage tools reduce review burden but introduce false-negative risk if not properly benchmarked against normal nocturnal movement and false-positive sensor artifacts.
options: Hire additional scoring personnel (e.g., sleep technologists) to achieve dual-rater consensus without algorithmic filtering, preserving manual oversight but consuming €40–60K additional annually in salary and training.

Deploy the semi-automated event-triage tool early (by month 12) with sensitivity thresholds tuned conservatively to prioritize specificity, accepting longer setup time for algorithm validation but reducing downstream manual review load.

Implement a single-rater workflow with spot-checks by the second rater on 20–30% of events, accepting lower inter-rater reliability reporting but freeing personnel for participant care and reducing publication-ready confidence in event counts.
levers.review_lever: Adding scorers scales costs linearly; early semi-automation risks publishing preliminary methods before field-validation. Single-rater workflow with spot-checks reduces inter-rater reliability claims, weakening Aim 2 phenotyping conclusions and potentially delaying manuscript acceptance in high-impact journals.

levers.name: Participant Recruitment Selectivity and Event-Yield Risk
levers.consequences: Strict pre-admission screening (clinical interview, prior PSG, bed-partner collateral) reduces admissions of participants with false-positive self-reported parasomnias, improving event yield. Relaxing criteria increases sample size and recruitment speed but risks admitting participants with subclinical symptoms or mimics, inflating the 20% unproductive-admission ceiling and triggering mid-study recruitment reviews that disrupt enrollment momentum.
options: Require prior polysomnography confirming at least one parasomnia-consistent arousal and corroborating history from a bed partner, accepting slower recruitment but higher expected event capture and cleaner Aim 2 phenotyping data.

Admit on structured clinical interview and self-reported frequency alone, accepting higher unproductive admissions and risk of EOG/EMG artifact misinterpretation as parasomnia events, but enabling rapid enrollment to meet 50–70 target by month 24.

Adopt a two-cohort design: 'confirmed' participants with prior PSG and 'suspected' participants with clinical interview only, analyzed separately, allowing flexibility in enrollment pacing and providing methodological transparency about diagnostic certainty stratification.
levers.review_lever: Strict pre-screening slows recruitment and may miss subtle cases; loose criteria risk contamination of event counts with mimics. Two-cohort design adds analytical complexity and dilutes sample size per group, potentially weakening statistical power for Aim 2 phenotyping unless per-cohort targets are increased.

levers.name: Facility Expansion Timing and Operational Capacity
levers.consequences: Deferring expansion from 8 to 12 suites until pilot data (month 18–24) validates safety and annotation throughput allows staff learning and sustainable operations. Expanding early increases bed capacity and recruitment pace but risks over-committing the 3-person night-shift team if event rates or false-alarm annotation exceed baseline assumptions, degrading care quality and data annotation reliability.
options: Expand to 12 suites by month 12 using the same 3-person team with external night-on-call backup and lean staffing ratios, accepting higher incident risk and potential annotation delays if event volume spikes.

Remain at 8 suites through month 30, investing only in second-rater staffing and algorithm development, ensuring operational stability and high inter-rater reliability but potentially missing 15–20 additional participant enrollment opportunities needed for Aim 2 statistical power.

Phase expansion to 10 suites by month 18 and 12 suites by month 24, contingent on meeting intermediate milestones (zero serious incidents, annotation backlog under two days), allowing flexible scale-up aligned with demonstrated operational capacity.
levers.review_lever: Early expansion risks incident and annotation quality; staying at 8 suites limits recruitment and may under-power Aim 2 analysis. Phased expansion with intermediate gates is pragmatic but requires rigorous milestone definition and discipline to halt expansion if thresholds are unmet mid-project.

levers.name: Funding Independence and Pharmaceutical Partnership Framing
levers.consequences: Retaining full independence under DFG and University of Bonn funding preserves publication autonomy and avoids perception of bias, but constrains upside funding and may require difficult cost-control decisions if recruitment or event capture lags assumptions. A pharma partnership secures budget flexibility and potential extension funding but introduces conflict-of-interest perception, even with a 30-day pre-publication window, potentially affecting journal acceptance and investigator credibility in the parasomnia research community.
options: Decline pharmaceutical partnership and manage all shortfalls through conservative recruitment pacing and extended timelines, accepting slower progress but ensuring unambiguous academic independence and publication momentum independent of industry approval.

Establish a pharma partnership early (month 3–6) with explicit contractual pre-publication comment window and publication-veto exclusions, accelerating budget certainty and enabling month-24 expansion but risking reputational alignment with industry interests.

Pursue pharmaceutical partnership only if recruitment or event yield falls below 20% protocol ceiling by month 18, positioning pharma as a contingency funding lever rather than a foundational requirement, avoiding early commitment while preserving optionality.
levers.review_lever: Full independence ensures credibility but constrains budget; early pharma partnership guarantees funding but invites bias perception. Contingency-based partnership delays certainty and may arrive too late to influence mid-course protocol adjustments, creating operational risk if month-18 milestones are missed.

levers.name: Data Sharing Strategy and Repository Selectivity
levers.consequences: Depositing de-identified physiological data in a recognized public repository accelerates secondary research and demonstrates scientific stewardship, advancing the field. However, selecting a repository with inadequate metadata standards or governance creates compliance risk; excluding bedroom video due to privacy constraints limits multimodal analyses by external groups, potentially reducing the dataset's reuse value and downstream citations.
options: Deposit all non-video streams (EEG, EOG, EMG, sensor data) in OpenNeuro or similar BIDS-compliant repository by month 36, with detailed documentation and usage metrics, maximizing visibility and reuse but accepting that external researchers cannot perform full-suite multimodal reanalysis.

Establish a restricted-access institutional repository with data use agreements for qualified researchers, maintaining tighter governance and allowing video inclusion under privacy-protective agreements, but reducing discoverability and slowing secondary research uptake.

Deposit a temporally and spatially downsampled physiological dataset (30-second epochs, compressed EEG) with video-free metadata in OpenNeuro, retaining full-resolution data only for internal Aim 3 algorithm development, balancing openness with privacy and reducing reuse complexity.
levers.review_lever: Public BIDS repository maximizes reuse and impact but excludes video; restricted-access repository preserves privacy but limits secondary research velocity. Downsampled public data retains openness but may be too coarse for external algorithm refinement, defeating the secondary-research goal and concentrating value within the local team.

responses.strategic_rationale: This residential parasomnia unit navigates four core tensions: (1) ecological validity versus clinical control — the domestic setting suppresses pathology while full PSG requires clinical rigor; (2) data richness versus annotation workload — tiered sensing captures infrequent events but strains manual scoring; (3) participant selectivity versus event yield — strict exclusions ensure safety and diagnostic clarity but limit enrollment and reduce statistical power; (4) operational sustainability versus facility expansion — proving the 8-suite model's safety and yield before scaling mitigates capital waste and staffing risk. The selected levers prioritize early-stage feasibility: demonstrating sustainable operations, optimizing the recruitment funnel, managing the annotation bottleneck through semi-automation, and staging financial commitments to gate risk. These choices reflect the reality that a methods-validation facility must first prove it can operate safely and produce usable data before pursuing scientific scope expansion or pharmaceutical partnerships.

levers.name: Domestic Staging Realism versus Incident Response Readiness
levers.consequences: Preserving naturalistic behavior through residential ambience reduces stimulus-induced suppression of parasomnia events, directly improving capture likelihood. However, padded corridors and silent alarms create a competing design tension: excessive safety markup converts the setting into a clinical facility, paradoxically defeating the naturalism goal while complicating rapid incident response if a participant is in genuine distress.
options: Deploy unobtrusive passive infrared motion detection with staff alert thresholds calibrated to actual fall or collision events rather than all movement, preserving ambient calm while enabling rapid 30-second response.

Install a separate clinical-grade safety observation suite adjacent to the main residential area so high-risk admissions or escalation nights use clinical infrastructure without contaminating the naturalistic dormitory environment.

Retain the residential aesthetic but conduct a 4-week mock-stay with trained confederate-actors simulating parasomnia behaviors to validate response times and staff coordination before enrolling real participants.
levers.review_lever: Domestic comfort and safety readiness operate on opposite gradients; overstating the ability to achieve both risks either naturalness loss or delayed incident response, particularly during extended overnight stays when staff fatigue compounds judgment errors.

levers.name: Technician Bottleneck and Real-Time Annotation Yield
levers.consequences: Each night technician annotates acutely observed events in real time, building the skeleton for dual-rater formal scoring later. This serves as the project's first quality gate and captures context (participant position, circadian phase, preceding EEG events) that video review alone misses. Bottleneck: three rotating technicians across eight suites mean each covers 2.7 suites per shift; a single complex night (multiple suspected events) can overwhelm annotation capacity and delay backup escalation-night triggering.
options: Hire a fourth part-time overnight technician dedicated solely to real-time annotation and escalation-night triggering, trading €15K year-one salary for elimination of the annotation queue backlog and faster algorithm-feedback loops.

Implement a structured technician checklist with a 10-minute maximum annotation window per suspected event, with longer annotations deferred to morning-shift review and escalation nights triggered only on motion-sensor consensus rather than technician judgment alone.

Adopt a 'floor technician plus annotation specialist' model where the night floor staff focuses on safety and basic event documentation, while a remote annotation specialist in a university office reviews sensor streams with 20-minute asynchronous delay and flags escalation nights via secure messaging.
levers.review_lever: Offloading annotation to asynchronous remote review introduces latency in escalation-night triggering and separates safety observation from physiological context, raising the risk that recurrent events are missed within the same stay.

levers.name: Recruitment Pipeline Tightness and Dropout-Adjusted Enrollment Capacity
levers.consequences: The specialist referral pathway (sleep clinic, neurology network, DGSM) ensures participants meet strict clinical criteria and reduces misclassification. Consequence: enrollment from three independent channels is heterogeneous — clinic referrals arrive pre-screened, while DGSM network referrals may have weaker documentation — and dropout risk varies by referral source. Assuming 30–35 admissions year two, a 15% dropout rate yields only 25–30 completed stays, falling short of Aim 2's phenotyping target of 50–70 participants over three years.
options: Negotiate a formal placement agreement with University Hospital Bonn's sleep clinic to dedicate one weekly specialist intake slot exclusively to parasomnia pre-screening, guaranteeing 40–50 pre-qualified candidates annually with documented prior polysomnography.

Expand recruitment to include German-language online sleep forums and patient advocacy groups for parasomnias, accepting lower pre-qualification rates but compensating with higher volume and participant self-selection that may reduce dropout.

Implement a phased-consent model where interested candidates enroll in a low-burden 2-night baseline visit at a partner outpatient clinic; only those completing baseline and confirming ≥1 captured episode enroll in the 2–8 week residential study, filtering out underestimators of event frequency before committed admission.
levers.review_lever: Online recruitment vastly broadens the candidate pool but introduces unvetted participants with higher diagnostic uncertainty and prior negative institutional experiences that increase dropout and complicate PI adjudication burden.

levers.name: Control Group Parity and Seasonal Recruitment Imbalance
levers.consequences: A matched-controls cohort (baseline movement, arousal, false-positive sensor activity) is essential for benchmarking event-triage sensitivity and specificity. Matching on age, sex, and sleep chronotype requires parallel enrollment and identical residential monitoring for 2–3 weeks per control. Bottleneck: recruiting healthy controls with stable sleep and no psychiatric or neurologic history is slower than patient recruitment because there is no referring clinical pipeline; controls self-refer through advertisements and university mailing lists, introducing long enrollment delays and potential seasonal clustering (summer holiday absences inflate spring/fall recruitment).
options: Recruit controls from University of Bonn employee populations and partner research institutions via institutional email campaigns, offering €800 lump compensation and guaranteed data destruction after study completion to address privacy concerns in a controlled referral network.

Pair each enrolled patient with an opportunistically recruited bed partner or household member as the control, matching naturally on cohabitation duration and circadian synchrony while reducing recruitment overhead by 50% and adding ecological validity to arousal-pattern baseline.

Stagger control enrollment to occur symmetrically across all three years in equal quarterly cohorts, accepting a 6-month delay in control-group completion for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis but securing year-round recruitment resilience and seasonal balance.
levers.review_lever: Pairing patients with household-member controls conflates control-group baseline with the patient's sleep environment and social factors, risking confounding in event-triage sensitivity estimates if controls inherit subclinical parasomnia traits from cohabitation.

levers.name: Escalation-Night Deployment Cadence and Algorithm Feedback Speed
levers.consequences: Full clinical-grade PSG on escalation nights post-event captures recurrence at the resolution needed for Aim 2 morphology and trigger analysis. Escalation is technician-triggered after a flagged event, ensuring targeted high-resolution capture rather than blanket nightly PSG (which would consume consumables and annotation time). Trade-off: technician judgment on 'flag-worthiness' is variable; a conservative threshold misses subtle recurrences, while a permissive threshold exhausts PSG electrode stock and delays formal scoring for months if the queue backlog grows.
options: Establish an algorithmic escalation rule: trigger full PSG automatically after any motion-sensor event exceeding a 95th-percentile amplitude threshold for that participant, removing technician subjectivity and enabling consistent algorithm-refinement feedback within weeks rather than months.

Reserve escalation-night PSG only for the first three suspected events per participant, after which analysis pivots to high-resolution video and ambient sensor review, preserving PSG consumables for new admissions and preventing algorithm overfitting to individual idiosyncrasies.

Conduct a weekly remote safety review where the PI and postdoctoral researchers audit all flagged events from the prior week via video and sensor playback; escalation nights are approved only for events meeting a consensus 'high morphological interest' criterion, introducing expert oversight but adding 7-day latency.
levers.review_lever: Algorithmic auto-escalation removes human judgment but risks saturating PSG capacity with borderline or false-positive events; consensus-review escalation ensures quality but delays recapture by a week, potentially missing within-stay recurrence windows that cluster episodically.

levers.name: Funding Contingency Gating and Pharmaceutical Partnership Optionality
levers.consequences: Year three funding is conditional on month-24 progress milestones (25+ participants, 40+ adjudicated events, publications). Pharmaceutical upside is a 30-day pre-publication comment window, preserving academic independence. Direct consequence: year one and two funding from DFG and University of Bonn internal sources is committed regardless of progress, allowing launch even if recruitment falters initially. Trade-off: if month-18 external review flags slow recruitment or low event yield, conditional year-three funding may vanish while committed year-one and two costs accumulate, stranding the program in mid-execution with no completion path.
options: Secure a committed no-strings year-three bridge from University of Bonn in month 12, independent of milestone achievement, in exchange for naming the unit and securing exclusive pre-publication access for university communications (preserving scientific independence while de-risking operational continuity).

Negotiate a pharma partnership in year one with a contractual commitment to fund year-three operations at €600K if internal milestones slip, accepting a second publication review cycle and modest equity in algorithm IP in exchange for institutional cash certainty.

Restructure the budget to front-load hiring and equipment in year one (€2.2M instead of €1.8M) and reduce year-two operational scope to 20–25 participants, allowing year three to serve as publication and grant-preparation phase with minimal operations cost, converting contingency into a reserve.
levers.review_lever: Pharma partnerships introduce publication friction and IP dilution even with a 30-day window; university bridge funding preserves control but relies on institutional commitment that can erode if university budget pressures spike mid-project.

levers.name: Event-Triage Algorithm Development Timeline and Convergence Risk
levers.consequences: Aim 3 requires a semi-automated event-triage tool benchmarked against dual human scorer agreement by month 36. Training requires a minimum labeled dataset of 200–300 independently scored events; based on 70–80% event-yield assumptions, 50–70 participants should yield 150–200 adjudicated events by month 24, leaving a 2–4 month window for algorithm training, validation, and writeup. Bottleneck: if event yield falls below 60% or dual-rater reliability drops below 80% agreement, the training dataset shrinks and algorithm performance cannot be benchmarked credibly, risking null or unpublishable results even if operations succeed.
options: Adopt a simplified event-triage approach based on motion-sensor amplitude and timing statistics alone (no deep learning) by month 18, allowing algorithm validation with as few as 80–100 labeled events and publication-ready results even if full dataset maturation lags.

Collaborate with a computational partner (e.g., Charité or Max Planck neuroinformatics group) to develop and validate the algorithm in parallel on retrospective nocturia and sleep apnea datasets, leveraging existing large corpora so Bonn data serves as external validation rather than primary training set.

Extend Aim 3 analysis to 18 months post-study (month 54 overall), formally separating algorithm development from the 36-month success criteria and positioning it as a secondary grant objective, reducing pressure to converge prematurely on a small event pool.
levers.review_lever: Simplifying to motion-sensor statistics loses the physiological nuance (EEG microarchitecture, arousal hierarchy) that distinguishes parasomnia from normal sleep micro-movements, trading methodological rigor for timeline certainty.

responses.strategic_rationale: The Bonn parasomnia unit operates at the intersection of clinical safety, operational complexity, and scientific yield. Core tensions center on balancing residential naturalism against incident detection, managing rare-event capture within fixed-duration stays, allocating limited technician capacity between real-time monitoring and annotation workload, and securing sustainable funding while maintaining academic independence. The seven levers below navigate these trade-offs by addressing: when to expand physical capacity, how to calibrate behavioral authenticity against sensor sensitivity, sequencing of algorithm development and human scorer training, timing and scope of data sharing versus privacy risk, staffing flexibility under variable event load, recruitment flexibility to maximize event yield within safety constraints, and contingency funding triggers that preserve research momentum without premature scaling.

levers.name: Residential Property Lease Terms and Expansion Optionality
levers.consequences: Long-term lease commitment enables stable operations and staff recruitment but creates multi-year fixed overhead regardless of enrollment velocity. Early lease renegotiation windows allow mid-course capacity scaling without capital loss, reducing the risk of under-utilization or overcrowding during pilot phase.
options: Negotiate 3-year lease with 2-year renewal option and suite-count escalation clauses, deferring expansion commitment until month 18 enrollment milestones are verified.
Secure long-term lease for all 12 suites upfront with staggered renovation and staffing, accepting higher early-stage burn to front-load operational readiness.
Establish rolling annual lease with property owner, preserving exit flexibility but risking relocation if enrollment ramps unexpectedly or neighborhood dynamics shift.
levers.review_lever: Early expansion optionality introduces landlord negotiation complexity and potential legal ambiguity, while upfront commitment ties capital to uncertain pilot success; annual rolling terms sacrifice stakeholder confidence and create recruitment instability.

levers.name: Technician Shift Coverage and Escalation-Night Staffing Model
levers.consequences: Three rotating technicians provide baseline safe coverage of 8 suites with event-annotation margin, but escalation nights with full PSG require additional real-time oversight, and unexpected high event loads exhaust annotation capacity. Staffing flexibility determines whether the team can respond to unpredictable event clusters without annotation backlog or staff burnout.
options: Hire a 4th on-call technician compensated for availability, escalating to active shifts when event frequency exceeds one flagged event per night for three consecutive nights.
Cross-train clinical psychologist and data engineer as backup annotators, enabling rapid response to high-load periods while preserving sleep medicine expertise during routine nights.
Establish a partnership with University Hospital Bonn's sleep lab for on-demand technician backfill during surges, formalizing a tiered subcontractor model with agreed response times.
levers.review_lever: On-call hiring adds fixed cost regardless of demand; cross-training dilutes expertise during critical annotation phases; hospital partnership risks competing priorities and delayed response when surge capacity is most needed.

levers.name: Enhanced-Night PSG Scheduling and Trigger-Based Escalation Protocol
levers.consequences: Fixed schedule of enhanced nights on day 1, mid-stay, and final night ensures systematic physiological documentation but may miss spontaneous events occurring outside these windows. Technician-triggered escalation nights capture recurrent events at clinical resolution but require real-time detection accuracy and create variable operational demand tied to episode frequency unpredictability.
options: Implement fixed 3-night enhanced schedule for all participants, with optional escalation nights only after human-verified event detection, prioritizing consistency and staff planning.

Deploy continuous low-burden sensing nightly with escalation to full PSG triggered within 2 hours of technician-flagged event, optimizing event-capture sensitivity at the cost of unpredictable staffing spikes.

Stratify enhanced-night scheduling by participant phenotype: frequent episodic participants (≥4 reported monthly episodes) receive 5 fixed enhanced nights; infrequent participants receive 3 fixed nights plus escalation.
levers.review_lever: Fixed scheduling risks missing rare clustered events and biasing characterization; pure escalation creates resource volatility and assumes technician detection accuracy under fatigue; stratification requires phenotype confirmation before enrollment, reducing adaptive flexibility.

levers.name: Event-Triage Algorithm Development and Validation Sequencing
levers.consequences: Algorithm development begins after collecting baseline annotated data (months 6–12), enabling training on real parasomnia morphology and false-positive patterns. Early deployment risks poor sensitivity and specificity, while delayed release defers tangible evidence of technical progress, affecting funding renewal confidence and publication timeline.
options: Release alpha algorithm by month 15 for internal technician use as a real-time ranking tool, gathering iterative feedback and refinement before formal peer-review validation.

Defer algorithm release until month 24, completing Aim 2 characterization and independent dual-scorer agreement first, ensuring validation against mature ground truth rather than provisional annotations.
Develop algorithm in parallel with a holdout test cohort (10–15 participants) beginning month 12, finalizing formal sensitivity–specificity estimates by month 20 for manuscript submission.
levers.review_lever: Early alpha deployment risks publishing performance claims on biased internal data; deferred release delays publications and weakens year-three funding renewal arguments; parallel holdout cohort extends enrollment timeline and increases per-participant cost without improving scientific validity.

levers.name: De-Identified Data Sharing Scope and Repository Selection
levers.consequences: Restricted sharing to physiological and environmental data under data use agreements preserves privacy compliance but limits research reproducibility and external collaboration opportunities. Broader de-identification and public deposition accelerate secondary analyses and increase citation impact, yet tighter anonymization protocols add processing overhead and potential data distortion.
options: Deposit raw PSG, actigraphy, and sensor data (excluding video) in an established sleep research repository (e.g., physionet) with participant consent to open-access sharing, accepting minimal residual privacy risk.

Implement custom tiered access: sensor and physiological data publicly available, video-derived behavioral features shared only under formal data use agreements with institutional review, balancing openness with privacy.

Restrict all data to local institutional access during the 3-year study and commit to full public release only after a 2-year embargo period, prioritizing proprietary value for upcoming funding applications.
levers.review_lever: Full open access maximizes research reach but creates irreversible privacy exposure if de-identification fails; tiered access adds administrative overhead without meaningfully reducing risk; embargo delays community contribution and weakens competitive positioning for secondary-data analyses.

levers.name: Participant Selection Stringency and Event-Yield Guarantee Risk
levers.consequences: Strict pre-admission screening (collateral history, prior PSG, structured exclusion checklist) reduces enrollment of borderline cases but improves event-capture probability and safety outcomes. Relaxed criteria accelerate recruitment but increase the likelihood of unproductive admissions lacking captured events within the 10-week window, depleting participant compensation budget and delaying longitudinal phenotyping.
options: Enforce rigid pre-screening requiring confirmed prior polysomnography and collateral bed-partner corroboration, accepting slower recruitment to maximize event-yield and minimize zero-capture admissions below the 20% protocol ceiling.

Adopt flexible pre-screening accepting clinical interview and self-report alone, with extended stay windows (up to 10 weeks) to capture rare events, front-loading recruitment velocity at the cost of higher participant costs and annotation delays.

Implement a two-tier recruitment pathway: fast-track streamlined enrollment for high-confidence referrals from University Hospital sleep clinic (80% of slots), reserve 20% for exploratory cases with relaxed criteria, creating a pilot-within-pilot cohort.
levers.review_lever: Rigid screening shrinks the eligible population and delays Aim 2 enrollment targets; flexible criteria inflate stay costs and annotation backlog; tiered approach segments the cohort, complicating between-person statistical modeling and diluting phenotypic homogeneity.

levers.name: Pharmaceutical Partnership Engagement Timing and Publication Rights Preservation
levers.consequences: Early pharma partnership (year one) secures optional upside funding and increases commercial visibility, but requires management overhead and introduces potential publication delays through pre-release review periods. Deferring partnership until year two allows independent proof-of-concept publications first, preserving academic primacy but risking missed funding and collaboration windows.
options: Secure partnership letters-of-intent by month 6, negotiating explicit non-exclusive rights and 30-day comment-only review windows now, front-loading commercial relationships while protecting publication independence.

Defer pharma outreach until month 18, after first peer-reviewed publications establish scientific credibility and independent funding sustainability, approaching partnerships from a position of demonstrated data quality.

Decline pharma partnership entirely, relying exclusively on DFG and university funding, accepting constrained upside scaling potential but eliminating all commercial influence and partner-driven operational pressure.
levers.review_lever: Early partnership risks publication friction and internal pressure to prioritize partner interests; deferred engagement may close funding opportunities and cede market awareness to competitors; partnership refusal limits resource flexibility if year-two enrollment trails targets.

levers.name: Facility Expansion Timing and Operational Capacity
levers.consequences: Deferring expansion from 8 to 12 suites until pilot data (month 18–24) validates safety and annotation throughput allows staff learning and sustainable operations. Expanding early increases bed capacity and recruitment pace but risks over-committing the 3-person night-shift team if event rates or false-alarm annotation exceed baseline assumptions, degrading care quality and data annotation reliability.
options: Expand to 12 suites by month 12 using the same 3-person team with external night-on-call backup and lean staffing ratios, accepting higher incident risk and potential annotation delays if event volume spikes.

Remain at 8 suites through month 30, investing only in second-rater staffing and algorithm development, ensuring operational stability and high inter-rater reliability but potentially missing 15–20 additional participant enrollment opportunities needed for Aim 2 statistical power.

Phase expansion to 10 suites by month 18 and 12 suites by month 24, contingent on meeting intermediate milestones (zero serious incidents, annotation backlog under two days), allowing flexible scale-up aligned with demonstrated operational capacity.
levers.review: Early expansion risks incident and annotation quality; staying at 8 suites limits recruitment and may under-power Aim 2 analysis. Phased expansion with intermediate gates is pragmatic but requires rigorous milestone definition and discipline to halt expansion if thresholds are unmet mid-project.

levers.name: Funding Independence and Pharmaceutical Partnership Framing
levers.consequences: Retaining full independence under DFG and University of Bonn funding preserves publication autonomy and avoids perception of bias, but constrains upside funding and may require difficult cost-control decisions if recruitment or event capture lags assumptions. A pharma partnership secures budget flexibility and potential extension funding but introduces conflict-of-interest perception, even with a 30-day pre-publication window, potentially affecting journal acceptance and investigator credibility in the parasomnia research community.
options: Decline pharmaceutical partnership and manage all shortfalls through conservative recruitment pacing and extended timelines, accepting slower progress but ensuring unambiguous academic independence and publication momentum independent of industry approval.

Establish a pharma partnership early (month 3–6) with explicit contractual pre-publication comment window and publication-veto exclusions, accelerating budget certainty and enabling month-24 expansion but risking reputational alignment with industry interests.

Pursue pharmaceutical partnership only if recruitment or event yield falls below 20% protocol ceiling by month 18, positioning pharma as a contingency funding lever rather than a foundational requirement, avoiding early commitment while preserving optionality.
levers.review: Full independence ensures credibility but constrains budget; early pharma partnership guarantees funding but invites bias perception. Contingency-based partnership delays certainty and may arrive too late to influence mid-course protocol adjustments, creating operational risk if month-18 milestones are missed.

levers.name: Data Sharing Strategy and Repository Selectivity
levers.consequences: Depositing de-identified physiological data in a recognized public repository accelerates secondary research and demonstrates scientific stewardship, advancing the field. However, selecting a repository with inadequate metadata standards or governance creates compliance risk; excluding bedroom video due to privacy constraints limits multimodal analyses by external groups, potentially reducing the dataset's reuse value and downstream citations.
options: Deposit all non-video streams (EEG, EOG, EMG, sensor data) in OpenNeuro or similar BIDS-compliant repository by month 36, with detailed documentation and usage metrics, maximizing visibility and reuse but accepting that external researchers cannot perform full-suite multimodal reanalysis.

Establish a restricted-access institutional repository with data use agreements for qualified researchers, maintaining tighter governance and allowing video inclusion under privacy-protective agreements, but reducing discoverability and slowing secondary research uptake.

Deposit a temporally and spatially downsampled physiological dataset (30-second epochs, compressed EEG) with video-free metadata in OpenNeuro, retaining full-resolution data only for internal Aim 3 algorithm development, balancing openness with privacy and reducing reuse complexity.
levers.review: Public BIDS repository maximizes reuse and impact but excludes video; restricted-access repository preserves privacy but limits secondary research velocity. Downsampled public data retains openness but may be too coarse for external algorithm refinement, defeating the secondary-research goal and concentrating value within the local team.

levers.name: Domestic Staging Realism versus Incident Response Readiness
levers.consequences: Preserving naturalistic behavior through residential ambience reduces stimulus-induced suppression of parasomnia events, directly improving capture likelihood. However, padded corridors and silent alarms create a competing design tension: excessive safety markup converts the setting into a clinical facility, paradoxically defeating the naturalism goal while complicating rapid incident response if a participant is in genuine distress.
options: Deploy unobtrusive passive infrared motion detection with staff alert thresholds calibrated to actual fall or collision events rather than all movement, preserving ambient calm while enabling rapid 30-second response.

Install a separate clinical-grade safety observation suite adjacent to the main residential area so high-risk admissions or escalation nights use clinical infrastructure without contaminating the naturalistic dormitory environment.

Retain the residential aesthetic but conduct a 4-week mock-stay with trained confederate-actors simulating parasomnia behaviors to validate response times and staff coordination before enrolling real participants.
levers.review: Domestic comfort and safety readiness operate on opposite gradients; overstating the ability to achieve both risks either naturalness loss or delayed incident response, particularly during extended overnight stays when staff fatigue compounds judgment errors.

levers.name: Technician Bottleneck and Real-Time Annotation Yield
levers.consequences: Each night technician annotates acutely observed events in real time, building the skeleton for dual-rater formal scoring later. This serves as the project's first quality gate and captures context (participant position, circadian phase, preceding EEG events) that video review alone misses. Bottleneck: three rotating technicians across eight suites mean each covers 2.7 suites per shift; a single complex night (multiple suspected events) can overwhelm annotation capacity and delay backup escalation-night triggering.
options: Hire a fourth part-time overnight technician dedicated solely to real-time annotation and escalation-night triggering, trading €15K year-one salary for elimination of the annotation queue backlog and faster algorithm-feedback loops.

Implement a structured technician checklist with a 10-minute maximum annotation window per suspected event, with longer annotations deferred to morning-shift review and escalation nights triggered only on motion-sensor consensus rather than technician judgment alone.

Adopt a 'floor technician plus annotation specialist' model where the night floor staff focuses on safety and basic event documentation, while a remote annotation specialist in a university office reviews sensor streams with 20-minute asynchronous delay and flags escalation nights via secure messaging.
levers.review: Offloading annotation to asynchronous remote review introduces latency in escalation-night triggering and separates safety observation from physiological context, raising the risk that recurrent events are missed within the same stay.

levers.name: Recruitment Pipeline Tightness and Dropout-Adjusted Enrollment Capacity
levers.consequences: The specialist referral pathway (sleep clinic, neurology network, DGSM) ensures participants meet strict clinical criteria and reduces misclassification. Consequence: enrollment from three independent channels is heterogeneous — clinic referrals arrive pre-screened, while DGSM network referrals may have weaker documentation — and dropout risk varies by referral source. Assuming 30–35 admissions year two, a 15% dropout rate yields only 25–30 completed stays, falling short of Aim 2's phenotyping target of 50–70 participants over three years.
options: Negotiate a formal placement agreement with University Hospital Bonn's sleep clinic to dedicate one weekly specialist intake slot exclusively to parasomnia pre-screening, guaranteeing 40–50 pre-qualified candidates annually with documented prior polysomnography.

Expand recruitment to include German-language online sleep forums and patient advocacy groups for parasomnias, accepting lower pre-qualification rates but compensating with higher volume and participant self-selection that may reduce dropout.

Implement a phased-consent model where interested candidates enroll in a low-burden 2-night baseline visit at a partner outpatient clinic; only those completing baseline and confirming ≥1 captured episode enroll in the 2–8 week residential study, filtering out underestimators of event frequency before committed admission.
levers.review: Online recruitment vastly broadens the candidate pool but introduces unvetted participants with higher diagnostic uncertainty and prior negative institutional experiences that increase dropout and complicate PI adjudication burden.

levers.name: Control Group Parity and Seasonal Recruitment Imbalance
levers.consequences: A matched-controls cohort (baseline movement, arousal, false-positive sensor activity) is essential for benchmarking event-triage sensitivity and specificity. Matching on age, sex, and sleep chronotype requires parallel enrollment and identical residential monitoring for 2–3 weeks per control. Bottleneck: recruiting healthy controls with stable sleep and no psychiatric or neurologic history is slower than patient recruitment because there is no referring clinical pipeline; controls self-refer through advertisements and university mailing lists, introducing long enrollment delays and potential seasonal clustering (summer holiday absences inflate spring/fall recruitment).
options: Recruit controls from University of Bonn employee populations and partner research institutions via institutional email campaigns, offering €800 lump compensation and guaranteed data destruction after study completion to address privacy concerns in a controlled referral network.

Pair each enrolled patient with an opportunistically recruited bed partner or household member as the control, matching naturally on cohabitation duration and circadian synchrony while reducing recruitment overhead by 50% and adding ecological validity to arousal-pattern baseline.

Stagger control enrollment to occur symmetrically across all three years in equal quarterly cohorts, accepting a 6-month delay in control-group completion for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis but securing year-round recruitment resilience and seasonal balance.
levers.review: Pairing patients with household-member controls conflates control-group baseline with the patient's sleep environment and social factors, risking confounding in event-triage sensitivity estimates if controls inherit subclinical parasomnia traits from cohabitation.

levers.name: Escalation-Night Deployment Cadence and Algorithm Feedback Speed
levers.consequences: Full clinical-grade PSG on escalation nights post-event captures recurrence at the resolution needed for Aim 2 morphology and trigger analysis. Escalation is technician-triggered after a flagged event, ensuring targeted high-resolution capture rather than blanket nightly PSG (which would consume consumables and annotation time). Trade-off: technician judgment on 'flag-worthiness' is variable; a conservative threshold misses subtle recurrences, while a permissive threshold exhausts PSG electrode stock and delays formal scoring for months if the queue backlog grows.
options: Establish an algorithmic escalation rule: trigger full PSG automatically after any motion-sensor event exceeding a 95th-percentile amplitude threshold for that participant, removing technician subjectivity and enabling consistent algorithm-refinement feedback within weeks rather than months.

Reserve escalation-night PSG only for the first three suspected events per participant, after which analysis pivots to high-resolution video and ambient sensor review, preserving PSG consumables for new admissions and preventing algorithm overfitting to individual idiosyncrasies.

Conduct a weekly remote safety review where the PI and postdoctoral researchers audit all flagged events from the prior week via video and sensor playback; escalation nights are approved only for events meeting a consensus 'high morphological interest' criterion, introducing expert oversight but adding 7-day latency.
levers.review: Algorithmic auto-escalation removes human judgment but risks saturating PSG capacity with borderline or false-positive events; consensus-review escalation ensures quality but delays recapture by a week, potentially missing within-stay recurrence windows that cluster episodically.

levers.name: Funding Contingency Gating and Pharmaceutical Partnership Optionality
levers.consequences: Year three funding is conditional on month-24 progress milestones (25+ participants, 40+ adjudicated events, publications). Pharmaceutical upside is a 30-day pre-publication comment window, preserving academic independence. Direct consequence: year one and two funding from DFG and University of Bonn internal sources is committed regardless of progress, allowing launch even if recruitment falters initially. Trade-off: if month-18 external review flags slow recruitment or low event yield, conditional year-three funding may vanish while committed year-one and two costs accumulate, stranding the program in mid-execution with no completion path.
options: Secure a committed no-strings year-three bridge from University of Bonn in month 12, independent of milestone achievement, in exchange for naming the unit and securing exclusive pre-publication access for university communications (preserving scientific independence while de-risking operational continuity).

Negotiate a pharma partnership in year one with a contractual commitment to fund year-three operations at €600K if internal milestones slip, accepting a second publication review cycle and modest equity in algorithm IP in exchange for institutional cash certainty.

Restructure the budget to front-load hiring and equipment in year one (€2.2M instead of €1.8M) and reduce year-two operational scope to 20–25 participants, allowing year three to serve as publication and grant-preparation phase with minimal operations cost, converting contingency into a reserve.
levers.review: Pharma partnerships introduce publication friction and IP dilution even with a 30-day window; university bridge funding preserves control but relies on institutional commitment that can erode if university budget pressures spike mid-project.

levers.name: Event-Triage Algorithm Development Timeline and Convergence Risk
levers.consequences: Aim 3 requires a semi-automated event-triage tool benchmarked against dual human scorer agreement by month 36. Training requires a minimum labeled dataset of 200–300 independently scored events; based on 70–80% event-yield assumptions, 50–70 participants should yield 150–200 adjudicated events by month 24, leaving a 2–4 month window for algorithm training, validation, and writeup. Bottleneck: if event yield falls below 60% or dual-rater reliability drops below 80% agreement, the training dataset shrinks and algorithm performance cannot be benchmarked credibly, risking null or unpublishable results even if operations succeed.
options: Adopt a simplified event-triage approach based on motion-sensor amplitude and timing statistics alone (no deep learning) by month 18, allowing algorithm validation with as few as 80–100 labeled events and publication-ready results even if full dataset maturation lags.

Collaborate with a computational partner (e.g., Charité or Max Planck neuroinformatics group) to develop and validate the algorithm in parallel on retrospective nocturia and sleep apnea datasets, leveraging existing large corpora so Bonn data serves as external validation rather than primary training set.

Extend Aim 3 analysis to 18 months post-study (month 54 overall), formally separating algorithm development from the 36-month success criteria and positioning it as a secondary grant objective, reducing pressure to converge prematurely on a small event pool.
levers.review: Simplifying to motion-sensor statistics loses the physiological nuance (EEG microarchitecture, arousal hierarchy) that distinguishes parasomnia from normal sleep micro-movements, trading methodological rigor for timeline certainty.

levers.name: Residential Property Lease Terms and Expansion Optionality
levers.consequences: Long-term lease commitment enables stable operations and staff recruitment but creates multi-year fixed overhead regardless of enrollment velocity. Early lease renegotiation windows allow mid-course capacity scaling without capital loss, reducing the risk of under-utilization or overcrowding during pilot phase.
options: Negotiate 3-year lease with 2-year renewal option and suite-count escalation clauses, deferring expansion commitment until month 18 enrollment milestones are verified.
Secure long-term lease for all 12 suites upfront with staggered renovation and staffing, accepting higher early-stage burn to front-load operational readiness.
Establish rolling annual lease with property owner, preserving exit flexibility but risking relocation if enrollment ramps unexpectedly or neighborhood dynamics shift.
levers.review: Early expansion optionality introduces landlord negotiation complexity and potential legal ambiguity, while upfront commitment ties capital to uncertain pilot success; annual rolling terms sacrifice stakeholder confidence and create recruitment instability.

levers.name: Technician Shift Coverage and Escalation-Night Staffing Model
levers.consequences: Three rotating technicians provide baseline safe coverage of 8 suites with event-annotation margin, but escalation nights with full PSG require additional real-time oversight, and unexpected high event loads exhaust annotation capacity. Staffing flexibility determines whether the team can respond to unpredictable event clusters without annotation backlog or staff burnout.
options: Hire a 4th on-call technician compensated for availability, escalating to active shifts when event frequency exceeds one flagged event per night for three consecutive nights.
Cross-train clinical psychologist and data engineer as backup annotators, enabling rapid response to high-load periods while preserving sleep medicine expertise during routine nights.
Establish a partnership with University Hospital Bonn's sleep lab for on-demand technician backfill during surges, formalizing a tiered subcontractor model with agreed response times.
levers.review: On-call hiring adds fixed cost regardless of demand; cross-training dilutes expertise during critical annotation phases; hospital partnership risks competing priorities and delayed response when surge capacity is most needed.

levers.name: Enhanced-Night PSG Scheduling and Trigger-Based Escalation Protocol
levers.consequences: Fixed schedule of enhanced nights on day 1, mid-stay, and final night ensures systematic physiological documentation but may miss spontaneous events occurring outside these windows. Technician-triggered escalation nights capture recurrent events at clinical resolution but require real-time detection accuracy and create variable operational demand tied to episode frequency unpredictability.
options: Implement fixed 3-night enhanced schedule for all participants, with optional escalation nights only after human-verified event detection, prioritizing consistency and staff planning.

Deploy continuous low-burden sensing nightly with escalation to full PSG triggered within 2 hours of technician-flagged event, optimizing event-capture sensitivity at the cost of unpredictable staffing spikes.

Stratify enhanced-night scheduling by participant phenotype: frequent episodic participants (≥4 reported monthly episodes) receive 5 fixed enhanced nights; infrequent participants receive 3 fixed nights plus escalation.
levers.review: Fixed scheduling risks missing rare clustered events and biasing characterization; pure escalation creates resource volatility and assumes technician detection accuracy under fatigue; stratification requires phenotype confirmation before enrollment, reducing adaptive flexibility.

levers.name: Event-Triage Algorithm Development and Validation Sequencing
levers.consequences: Algorithm development begins after collecting baseline annotated data (months 6–12), enabling training on real parasomnia morphology and false-positive patterns. Early deployment risks poor sensitivity and specificity, while delayed release defers tangible evidence of technical progress, affecting funding renewal confidence and publication timeline.
options: Release alpha algorithm by month 15 for internal technician use as a real-time ranking tool, gathering iterative feedback and refinement before formal peer-review validation.

Defer algorithm release until month 24, completing Aim 2 characterization and independent dual-scorer agreement first, ensuring validation against mature ground truth rather than provisional annotations.
Develop algorithm in parallel with a holdout test cohort (10–15 participants) beginning month 12, finalizing formal sensitivity–specificity estimates by month 20 for manuscript submission.
levers.review: Early alpha deployment risks publishing performance claims on biased internal data; deferred release delays publications and weakens year-three funding renewal arguments; parallel holdout cohort extends enrollment timeline and increases per-participant cost without improving scientific validity.

levers.name: De-Identified Data Sharing Scope and Repository Selection
levers.consequences: Restricted sharing to physiological and environmental data under data use agreements preserves privacy compliance but limits research reproducibility and external collaboration opportunities. Broader de-identification and public deposition accelerate secondary analyses and increase citation impact, yet tighter anonymization protocols add processing overhead and potential data distortion.
options: Deposit raw PSG, actigraphy, and sensor data (excluding video) in an established sleep research repository (e.g., physionet) with participant consent to open-access sharing, accepting minimal residual privacy risk.

Implement custom tiered access: sensor and physiological data publicly available, video-derived behavioral features shared only under formal data use agreements with institutional review, balancing openness with privacy.

Restrict all data to local institutional access during the 3-year study and commit to full public release only after a 2-year embargo period, prioritizing proprietary value for upcoming funding applications.
levers.review: Full open access maximizes research reach but creates irreversible privacy exposure if de-identification fails; tiered access adds administrative overhead without meaningfully reducing risk; embargo delays community contribution and weakens competitive positioning for secondary-data analyses.

levers.name: Participant Selection Stringency and Event-Yield Guarantee Risk
levers.consequences: Strict pre-admission screening (collateral history, prior PSG, structured exclusion checklist) reduces enrollment of borderline cases but improves event-capture probability and safety outcomes. Relaxed criteria accelerate recruitment but increase the likelihood of unproductive admissions lacking captured events within the 10-week window, depleting participant compensation budget and delaying longitudinal phenotyping.
options: Enforce rigid pre-screening requiring confirmed prior polysomnography and collateral bed-partner corroboration, accepting slower recruitment to maximize event-yield and minimize zero-capture admissions below the 20% protocol ceiling.

Adopt flexible pre-screening accepting clinical interview and self-report alone, with extended stay windows (up to 10 weeks) to capture rare events, front-loading recruitment velocity at the cost of higher participant costs and annotation delays.

Implement a two-tier recruitment pathway: fast-track streamlined enrollment for high-confidence referrals from University Hospital sleep clinic (80% of slots), reserve 20% for exploratory cases with relaxed criteria, creating a pilot-within-pilot cohort.
levers.review: Rigid screening shrinks the eligible population and delays Aim 2 enrollment targets; flexible criteria inflate stay costs and annotation backlog; tiered approach segments the cohort, complicating between-person statistical modeling and diluting phenotypic homogeneity.

levers.name: Pharmaceutical Partnership Engagement Timing and Publication Rights Preservation
levers.consequences: Early pharma partnership (year one) secures optional upside funding and increases commercial visibility, but requires management overhead and introduces potential publication delays through pre-release review periods. Deferring partnership until year two allows independent proof-of-concept publications first, preserving academic primacy but risking missed funding and collaboration windows.
options: Secure partnership letters-of-intent by month 6, negotiating explicit non-exclusive rights and 30-day comment-only review windows now, front-loading commercial relationships while protecting publication independence.

Defer pharma outreach until month 18, after first peer-reviewed publications establish scientific credibility and independent funding sustainability, approaching partnerships from a position of demonstrated data quality.

Decline pharma partnership entirely, relying exclusively on DFG and university funding, accepting constrained upside scaling potential but eliminating all commercial influence and partner-driven operational pressure.
levers.review: Early partnership risks publication friction and internal pressure to prioritize partner interests; deferred engagement may close funding opportunities and cede market awareness to competitors; partnership refusal limits resource flexibility if year-two enrollment trails targets.

6. **Length Limits**
   - Keep each `review_lever` to 20–40 words.

Plan:
Establish a 3-year residential longitudinal research unit in Bonn, Germany, for the study of adult NREM parasomnias — sleepwalking, confusional arousals, and sleep terrors — with a secondary exploratory arm for REM sleep behavior disorder under a separate protocol with dedicated neurologic screening, reflecting RBD's distinct clinical trajectory per current AASM guidance. The facility is affiliated with University Hospital Bonn's Department of Epileptology, leveraging its existing long-term video-EEG monitoring culture, and addresses a specific methodological gap: traditional single-night polysomnography rarely captures infrequent parasomnia events, while outpatient actigraphy lacks physiological resolution. The unit houses 8 active sleep suites at launch in a converted residential property in a quiet Bonn neighborhood, renovated for safety (padded corridor edges, restricted-opening windows, silent exterior door alarms, fire safety, acoustic treatment, network cabling, accessibility modifications) while preserving a domestic feel — if the environment is too clinical, naturalistic behavior is suppressed. Physical capacity exists for 12 suites, but expansion is deferred until the pilot proves acceptable data quality, manageable false alarm rates, safe staffing ratios, and usable annotation throughput. Sensing uses a tiered acquisition model: nightly low-burden monitoring via dry-electrode EEG headbands, contact-free mattress sensors, unobtrusively mounted infrared cameras, ambient microphones, and environmental sensors; scheduled enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage including standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, and leg EMG on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant; and escalation nights deploying full PSG after technician-flagged events to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution. All streams are time-synchronized and stored in EEG-BIDS-compatible format on a local NAS with nightly encrypted backup to university storage, annotated in real time by the night technician and later scored by two independent raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported. Public data sharing is limited to de-identified physiological and sensor data under data use agreements — bedroom video carries severe privacy constraints and is not deposited in public repositories. The scientific program has three explicit aims: Aim 1, establish and operationally validate the residential capture model as safe, ethics-approved, and sustainable; Aim 2, characterize within-person and between-person parasomnia patterns longitudinally, including episode frequency, morphology, triggers, and temporal clustering; Aim 3, develop and benchmark semi-automated event-triage tools that rank probable parasomnia episodes and reduce manual review burden, evaluated against dual human scorer agreement rather than promising autonomous diagnosis.

Participant recruitment targets adults aged 18–65 with NREM parasomnia confirmed through a structured pre-admission pathway: specialist clinical interview, collateral history from bed partner or household member where available, prior or screening polysomnography, and a structured exclusion checklist adjudicated by the PI. Explicit exclusions are nocturnal epilepsy or suspected epilepsy mimics, untreated obstructive sleep apnea, active major substance use disorder, severe psychiatric instability, and wandering or injury risk beyond facility capability. Recruitment channels are the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologist referrals, and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, with per-night compensation of €80 plus meals. A matched control group provides baseline nocturnal movement, arousal patterns, and false-positive sensor activity under identical residential monitoring conditions, enabling benchmarking of the event-triage tools against normal nocturnal behavior. Event-yield planning assumes that based on the inclusion criterion of at least 2 self-reported episodes per month, approximately 70–80% of admitted participants will produce at least one captured and adjudicated event during a 2–8 week stay; stays may be extended up to 2 additional weeks for participants with zero captured events after the initial period, capped at 10 weeks total, with a protocol ceiling of 20% unproductive admissions before triggering a recruitment-criteria review. The core team is 9 people: a PI who is a board-certified sleep medicine physician, 2 postdoctoral researchers in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience respectively, 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to ensure safe coverage of 8 active suites with adequate margin for event response and annotation, a clinical psychologist specializing in sleep disorders, a data engineer managing the sensor pipeline, and a study coordinator handling recruitment, consent, scheduling, and ethics compliance.

Budget is €3.8 million over 3 years, gated: €1.8M year one covering property lease and renovation at approximately €750K, equipment at approximately €450K, staff hiring accounting for German social insurance contributions and actual overnight coverage, ethics approval, and a pilot cohort of 15–20 participants; €1.2M year two covering full operations with 30–35 participants, the enhanced-night PSG program, first publications, and event-triage algorithm development; €800K year three conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24. Personnel costs are approximately €2M over three years and remaining funds cover participant compensation, independent scoring time, data storage and retention, regulatory and legal work, and contingency. Funding sources are DFG research grant and University of Bonn internal research funding as the primary pillars, with a pharmaceutical industry partnership as optional upside rather than a feasibility requirement — if secured, the academic team retains full publication rights with the pharma partner receiving a 30-day pre-publication comment window only. Success criteria at 36 months: safe residential monitoring operations sustained for at least 24 months, enrollment of 50–70 NREM parasomnia participants plus matched controls, capture of a prespecified minimum number of independently adjudicated parasomnia events sufficient for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis, 2–3 peer-reviewed publications in sleep medicine journals covering methods validation and longitudinal characterization, a benchmarked semi-automated event-triage model with reported sensitivity, specificity, and agreement against dual human scoring, de-identified physiological dataset deposited in a recognized repository, and a submitted phase-two grant proposal for expansion and intervention studies. Failure triggers: if by month 18 the facility has enrolled fewer than 25 participants or captured fewer than 40 adjudicated events, the program undergoes external review. Governance is a 3-member external scientific advisory board reviewing progress every 6 months, with the PI holding operational authority and budget reallocations above €50K requiring board approval. Banned words: AI, blockchain, app, VR, AR, gamification, wearable startup, consumer product, DAO, NFT, metaverse, smart home, autonomous diagnosis, digital therapeutic, SaaS, marketplace, validated (in the context of claiming a mature deployable system). Pick a realistic scenario — this is an early-stage clinical research facility producing methods validation and phenotyping work, not a finished diagnostic platform.
